questions.text: (a) From which end of the ovule, and how does the pollen tube gain its entry into the embryo sac of a Hibiscus flower ? (b) State the fate of the male nuclei present in the pollen tube.

answer.text:
(a) The pollen tube enters the ovule from the micropylar end and passes into a synergid, guided by the filiform apparatus.
(b) Double fertilisation: one male gamete fuses with the two polar nuclei to form the primary endosperm nucleus (triple fusion); the other male gamete fuses with the egg cell to form the zygote (syngamy).

questions.text: Study the diagram given below showing the modes of pollination. Answer the questions that follow. (i) The given diagram shows three methods of pollen transfer in plants. What are the technical terms used for pollen transfer methods '1', '2' and '3' ? (ii) How do the following plants achieve pollination successfully ? (1) Water lily (2) Vallisneria (iii) Flowering plants have developed many devices to avoid inbreeding depression. Explain one hereditary and one physiological device which helps plants to achieve this target.

answer.text:
(i) (1) Autogamy; (2) Geitonogamy; (3) Xenogamy.
(ii) (1) Water lily — pollinated by insects or wind.
(2) Vallisneria — the female flowers reach the water surface on long stalks; the male flowers or pollen are released onto the water and carried by the water current to the female flowers to achieve pollination.
(iii) Genetic (self-incompatibility): prevents the self-pollen of the same flower or plant from fertilising the ovules, by inhibiting pollen germination and pollen-tube growth in the pistil.
Physiological: pollen release and stigma receptivity are not synchronised — either the pollen matures earlier and the stigma later, or the pollen matures later than the stigma.

questions.text: (a) (i) Explain how does double fertilisation take place in a flowering plant. (ii) Write the fate of the products of double fertilization in these plants.

answer.text:
(a)
(i)
After entering one of the synergids the pollen tube releases the
two male gametes into the cytoplasm of the synergid, one of the male
gametes moves towards the egg cell and fuses with its nucleus thus
completing the syngamy to form zygote, the other male gamete moves
towards the two polar nuclei located in the central cell and fuses with it
causing triple fusion to form Primary endosperm nucleus (PEN)  or
Primary endosperm cell (PEC).
(ii)
Primary endosperm cell (PEC) and develops into the
endosperm, while the zygote develops into an embryo.

questions.text: (a) (i) Explain the structure of a mature embryo sac of a typical flowering plant. (ii) How is triple fusion achieved in these plants ?

answer.text:
(a)
(i) Three cells are grouped together at the micropylar end of embryo sac ,constitute
the egg apparatus, the egg apparatus in turn consists of two synergids , one egg cell,
the synergids have special cellular thickenings at the micropylar tip called filiform
apparatus, three cells are at the chalazal end and are called the antipodals, the large
central cell has two polar nuclei, thus a typical angiosperm embryo sac at maturity
though 8-nucleate is 7-celled.
(ii)One of the two male gametes fuses with the two polar nuclei located in the
central cell to produce a triploid primary endosperm nucleus (PEN).

(ii)
Compatible pollen grain germinates on the stigma to produce pollen tube that
grows through the tissues of stigma and style and reaches to the ovary
Generative cell divides into two male gametes while moving through style
and Pollen tube enters the ovule through the micropyle and then enters one of
the synergids through the filiform apparatus

forming a zygote (syngamy)
The other male gamete moves towards the two polar nuclei present in the
central cell and fuses with them to form Primary Endosperm Nucleus / PEN
(triple fusion).

Double Fertilization)

questions.text: Gene expresses itself in a cell system as a protein/enzyme. How does an expression of gene occur in a cell system and when does it need to occur, and how the gene expression is regulated in a prokaryote cell system was studied by the combined efforts of Jacque Monod, the biochemist and Francois Jacob, the geneticist. For their work on lactose metabolism in E. coli, by which they were able to elucidate the lac operon, they were awarded the Nobel Prize in 1965. (a) Why is lac operon said to be a transcriptionally regulated system ? (b) It is said that the lac operon has to be operational at a very low level in the bacterial cell all the time. Justify. (c) Why is the regulator gene in lac operon called so ? (d) Draw a schematic diagram of lac operon in absence of inducer in the culture medium of the bacteria. OR (d) Draw a schematic diagram of lac operon in the presence of inducer in the culture medium of the bacteria.

answer.text:
(a) In the presence of lactose the repressor protein does not bind to the operator region (O), so RNA polymerase is able to transcribe the operon.
In the absence of lactose the repressor protein binds to the operator region (O) and prevents RNA polymerase from transcribing the operon.
(b) The permease enzyme, coded by gene 'y', is required to let lactose enter the cell, so that the operon can be switched on.
(c) 'i' stands for the inhibitor (regulatory) gene; it transcribes the repressor protein, which binds to the operator site and switches the operon off.
(d) In the absence of an inducer: the i-gene forms repressor mRNA and then the repressor protein, which binds the operator and blocks RNA polymerase, so the structural genes z, y and a are not transcribed.
In the presence of an inducer: the inducer inactivates the repressor; RNA polymerase transcribes z, y and a into lac mRNA, which is translated into $\beta$-galactosidase, permease and transacetylase.

questions.text: Meselson and Stahl carried out an experiment to prove the nature of DNA replication. Recall the experiment and answer the following questions. (iii) State the role of caesium chloride density gradient in their experiment. (iv) Write the conclusions they arrived at.

answer.text:
Meselson and Stahl's experiment:
(i) Two types of DNA were produced — DNA with normal nitrogen ($^{14}$N, light) and DNA with heavy nitrogen ($^{15}$N, heavy).
(ii) E. coli has a generation time of about 20 minutes, so samples were taken at 20-minute intervals to follow the mode of replication after $^{15}$N-labelled E. coli was transferred to a $^{14}$N (normal) medium.
(iii) Centrifugation in a caesium chloride density gradient was used to distinguish/separate heavy DNA from light DNA on the basis of density.
(iv) The experiment showed that DNA replication is semiconservative.

questions.text: (a) (i) Describe the series of experiments conducted by Frederick Griffith. Comment on the significance of the result obtained. (ii) State the contribution of Avery, MacLeod and McCarty.

answer.text:
(a)
(i) Griffith worked on Streptococcus pneumoniae bacteria having two strains:
S strain (Smooth) with mucous (polysaccharide) coat was virulent/ pathogenic
R strain (Rough) has no coat and was non virulent/non pathogenic
Griffith took a Mice and injected these bacteria in a series of experiments
S strain → Inject into Mice → Mice Died
R strain → Inject into Mice → Mice live
He killed S strain bacteria with heat
S strain (heat killed) → Inject into Mice → Mice live
S strain (heat killed) + R strain (live) → Inject into mice → Mice die
He recovered living S bacteria from the body of dead mice.
Conclusion: Griffith concluded that some “transforming principle” transferred
from the heat-killed S strain, had enabled the R strain to synthesise a smooth
polysaccharide coat and become virulent due to the transfer of the genetic
material.
(ii)
MacLeod, MacCarty & Avery
They worked to determine the biochemical nature of “transforming
principle” in Griffith’s experiment.
They purified biochemical (DNA, RNA, protein etc) from heat killed S cells
to see which could transform live R cells into S cells.
They discovered that DNA alone from S cells transformed R cells.
They also discovered that protein digesting Proteases and RNA digesting
RNases did not affect transformation.
But when DNA was digested by DNase there was no transformation So DNA
is hereditary material.

questions.text: How does the process of Natural Selection affect Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium ? Explain with the help of graphs.

answer.text:
Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium: allele frequencies in a population stay constant across generations when no evolutionary force acts. Natural selection is a force that disturbs this equilibrium — it changes allele/genotype frequencies, so the population evolves. (Graphs of frequency vs phenotype):
• Stabilising selection: favours intermediate phenotypes, reduces variation (single central peak).
• Directional selection: favours one extreme phenotype, shifting the mean towards it.
• Disruptive selection: favours both extreme phenotypes over the mean, giving two peaks.
Because selected individuals contribute more offspring, allele frequencies change and Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium is not maintained.

questions.text: (a) How is Hardy-Weinberg expression (p² + 2pq + q²) = 1 derived ? (b) List any two factors that disturb the genetic equilibrium.

According to Hardy Weinberg principle –
Sum total of all the Allelic frequencies in a population  = 1.
Let there be two alleles A and a in the population. Let their frequencies be

p + q = 1
The frequency of AA will be p2 because - the probability that an allele A
with frequency ‘p’ would appear on both the chromosomes of a
diploid individual will be product of probabilities i.e. p2.
Similarly frequency of ‘a’ will be q2 ,
and Aa is 2pq
Hence p² + 2pq + q² = 1

questions.text: Treatment of wastewater is done in a sewage treatment plant to make it less polluting. Explain the following with reference to this treatment process : (a) Primary sludge (b) Activated sludge (c) Anaerobic sludge digesters

answer.text:
(a) Primary sludge: all the solids that settle down during the primary treatment of sewage water.
(b) Activated sludge: the sediment produced during the secondary (biological) treatment — the primary effluent together with aerobic microbial flocs (bacteria and fungi), whose BOD has been reduced significantly.
(c) Anaerobic sludge digesters: large tanks in which the activated sludge is digested by anaerobic bacteria, producing a mixture of $CH_4$, $H_2S$ and $CO_2$ (biogas).

questions.text: With the help of a schematic diagram only, show in three steps, the formation of recombinant DNA by the action of restriction endonuclease — EcoRI and DNA ligase.

answer.text:
Formation of recombinant DNA using the restriction enzyme EcoRI:
• EcoRI cuts both the vector DNA and the foreign DNA at the same palindromic recognition sequence, $5'$-GAATTC-$3'$, between G and A on each strand.
• This staggered cut leaves complementary single-stranded 'sticky ends' (AATT overhangs) on both DNA molecules.
• The sticky end of the foreign DNA base-pairs with the complementary sticky end of the vector DNA.
• DNA ligase then seals the joins to produce the recombinant DNA molecule.

questions.text: (b) Explain the amplification of gene of interest using the technique of Polymerase chain reaction (PCR).

answer.text:
(b)
· Each cycle in PCR has three steps:
Denaturation, Annealing, Extension
− Denaturation:  DNA subjected to higher temperature, the two
strands of DNA separate due to broken hydrogen bonds between
nitrogenous bases
− Annealing: Two sets of primers, which are complementary
attach on 3’ end of both template strands.
− Extension: the new strand of DNA is formed using thermostable
Taq polymerase enzyme (derived from Thermus aquaticus
bacterium), extends the primers and the nucleotides provided in
the reaction and the genomic DNA act as the template.
− The process of replication of DNA is repeated 30 times the
segment of DNA is amplified 1 billion times i.e. 1 billion copies
are made.

diversity than Eastern Ghats / any other correct example.

types of ecosystems in a particular area.
e.g. India has a number of ecosystems like rain forests, coral reefs, deserts  /
any other correct example.
